title: Foundations of Machine Learning
subtitle: From “what is learning?” to models you can defend
summary: A first serious course in machine learning: what a learning problem is, why generalization is the whole game, linear models derived from first principles, and the discipline of honest model selection. Every claim is derived or cited; nothing is hand-waved.
author: AI Mastery curriculum team
audience: Learners comfortable with single-variable calculus and basic linear algebra
objectives: State a learning problem as minimisation of population risk and explain why empirical risk is a proxy for it.
Derive the bias–variance decomposition for squared loss and use it to read a learning curve.
Derive the normal equations for least squares and solve them both in closed form and by gradient descent.
Explain how step size controls convergence of gradient descent on a quadratic, including divergence.
Design a model-selection protocol with cross-validation that avoids leakage.
prerequisitesNote: Comfort with derivatives and matrix–vector products. No prior machine learning assumed.
completionCriteria: Complete every lesson and score at least 70% of exercise points in the Problem Arena.

modules.title: What learning is, and what it costs
modules.summary: The vocabulary and the one quantity that matters: risk on data you have not seen.

lessons.title: What a learning problem actually is
lessons.summary: Population risk, empirical risk, and why the gap between them is the entire subject.

blocks.text: Three ingredients, no more

Every supervised learning problem you will ever meet is the same three objects in different clothing: a **distribution** $\mathcal{D}$ over inputs and outputs, a **hypothesis class** $\mathcal{H}$ of candidate predictors, and a **loss** $\ell$ that scores a prediction against the truth. Learning means using a finite sample from $\mathcal{D}$ to pick one $h \in \mathcal{H}$ that behaves well on draws from $\mathcal{D}$ you never saw.
The population risk (generalisation error) of a predictor $h$ is the expected loss on a fresh draw from the data-generating distribution.
Population risk is what we care about and what we can never compute: it is an expectation over a distribution we do not have, only samples from. The object we can compute is its sample average.

payload.label: empirical risk
payload.note: The empirical risk is a Monte Carlo estimate of the population risk for any fixed h.

blocks.text: Empirical risk minimisation (ERM) is the default learning principle: pick $h$ in $\mathcal{H}$ minimising $\hat{R}_n$. Everything else in this course is either a refinement of ERM (regularisation, early stopping) or an analysis of when it works (generalisation bounds).

payload.title: Why the empirical risk is a trustworthy proxy for a fixed predictor

steps.text: Fix any single $h$. The losses $\ell(h(x_i), y_i)$ are i.i.d. draws of a random variable with mean $R(h)$.
The sample mean is unbiased, so on average the empirical risk equals the population risk.
If the loss is bounded in $[0, M]$, Hoeffding's inequality gives a two-sided deviation bound for that fixed $h$.
steps.note: This is a statement about one fixed h, not about the h the algorithm chose.

steps.text: To cover the whole class, take a union bound over a finite $\mathcal{H}$: the price is a factor $|\mathcal{H}|$ inside the log.

payload.conclusion: Uniform control over a finite class costs $\log |\mathcal{H}|$ samples. For infinite classes the same role is played by capacity measures (VC dimension, Rademacher complexity, PAC-Bayes bounds) — the topic `statistical-learning-theory` in the map.

blocks.text: Read that conclusion carefully: the danger is not that $\hat{R}_n$ is a bad estimate for one predictor, but that we *search* over many predictors and report the best. Search is what turns a good estimator into an optimistic one.

A model that scores $0.02$ on the data it was fitted to and $0.31$ on held-out data has not failed to optimise — it has succeeded at optimising the wrong objective. The gap $R(h) - \hat{R}_n(h)$ is called the **generalisation gap**, and it grows with how hard you search, not with how well you fit.

items: **Distribution** $\mathcal{D}$: what “a new example” means. Changing it changes the problem.
**Hypothesis class** $\mathcal{H}$: what you were willing to consider. Constraints here are prior knowledge.
**Loss** $\ell$: what mistakes cost. Squared loss penalises outliers; 0–1 loss counts them.

payload.problem: A clinic records whether a patient returns within 30 days ($y \in \{0,1\}$) and you must predict it. Base rate: 18% return. Consider the constant predictor $h(x) = 0$ under 0–1 loss. What is its population risk, and what does that number mean?
steps: 0–1 loss of the constant-0 predictor is 1 exactly when $y = 1$ and 0 otherwise.
Any model you propose must beat 0.18 out-of-sample to have learned anything at all.
payload.answer: $R(h) = 0.18$. This is the **base-rate baseline**: the score of ignoring the features entirely. Report it next to every model score, always.
payload.note: Half of all disappointing model results in practice are a model that sits below its own base-rate baseline on held-out data.

questions.prompt: Why can we not simply minimise population risk directly?
options: Because it is an expectation over a distribution we only have samples from
Because it depends on the optimiser
questions.explain: Population risk is defined by an expectation over D. We observe n samples, so we minimise a sample average instead.

questions.prompt: The union bound over a finite hypothesis class shows the sample cost of uniform control grows with…
questions.explain: Solving 2|H|exp(-2nε²/M²) ≤ δ for n puts log|H| in the numerator.

items: I can write population risk and empirical risk from memory and say which one is computable.
I can explain in one sentence why searching over many hypotheses makes the empirical risk optimistic.
I can state the base-rate baseline for a binary problem and compute it from the class prior.

lessons.title: Generalization and the bias–variance tradeoff
lessons.summary: Deriving the decomposition, reading learning curves, and what double descent does and does not break.

blocks.text: One decomposition, two failure modes

Fix squared loss and a regression target $y = f(x) + \varepsilon$ with $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2$. The predictor you get depends on the *sample* you happened to draw, so treat $\hat{f}$ as a random function and average over samples.

payload.title: Bias–variance decomposition for squared loss

steps.text: Define the mean predictor over datasets of size $n$.
Expand the expected squared error at a point, adding and subtracting $\bar{f}(x)$.
The cross terms vanish because $\mathbb{E}_S[\hat{f}_S - \bar{f}] = 0$ and $\varepsilon$ is independent of $S$.
steps.note: This is the step people skip; it is why the decomposition is exact rather than approximate.

payload.conclusion: Expected error splits into how wrong the *average* fit is (bias), how much individual fits disagree (variance), and noise you cannot remove. Underfitting is bias; overfitting is variance.

payload.caption: The two ways to be wrong, and the lever that moves each.

items.title: High bias (underfitting)
items.summary: The class cannot express the target, so every dataset gives a similarly wrong answer.
points: Train error and test error are both high and close together
Fix: enlarge $\mathcal{H}$, add features, reduce regularisation
Example: fitting a straight line to a clearly curved response

items.title: High variance (overfitting)
items.summary: The class is rich enough to fit noise, so answers swing with the sample.
points: Train error low, test error high: a large generalisation gap
Fix: more data, regularisation, simpler class, ensembling
Example: a degree-40 polynomial through 30 noisy points

payload.problem: Fit polynomials of degree $d \in \{1, 3, 9, 20\}$ to $n = 40$ points from $y = \sin(2x) + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim N(0, 0.1^2)$. Predict the shape of the train-error and test-error curves as $d$ grows.
steps: Train error decreases monotonically in $d$: a richer class can always fit the sample at least as well.
Test error falls from $d=1$ to $d=3$ (bias drops faster than variance rises), then climbs: at $d=20$ the fit interpolates noise.
The test curve is U-shaped; the gap between the curves is the variance term made visible.
payload.answer: Monotone-decreasing train error, U-shaped test error, and a widening gap — the signature of the tradeoff.
payload.note: With n = 40 and d = 20 you have 21 parameters: interpolation territory, where classical theory predicts disaster.

blocks.text: Modern deep networks interpolate their training data and still generalise, and test error can fall again past the interpolation point (**double descent**). This does not refute the decomposition — it shows that variance is not monotone in raw parameter count. Capacity measures that track the *effective* flexibility of the fitted function remain the right lens; the topic `loss-landscapes-and-grokking` covers the current picture.

Practically, you will rarely compute bias and variance separately — you need many independent datasets for that. What you *can* see is the pair of learning curves: train and validation error against training-set size. Bias shows up as a high plateau both curves share; variance shows up as a gap that closes as $n$ grows.

questions.prompt: Train error 0.02, validation error 0.30, and both barely move when you add data. The dominant term is…
questions.explain: A large gap that shrinks with more data is variance. If the gap persists at large n, suspect leakage or distribution shift instead.

questions.prompt: Which term in the decomposition is unaffected by your modelling choices?
questions.explain: The label noise σ² is a property of D, not of H or the algorithm.

items: I can derive the bias–variance decomposition and say exactly where independence of the noise is used.
I can look at a train/validation curve pair and name the dominant error term.
I can state what double descent does and does not contradict.

modules.title: Linear models, end to end
modules.summary: Least squares derived twice — by calculus and by geometry — then solved by gradient descent with the step size made explicit.

lessons.title: Linear regression: from least squares to gradients
lessons.summary: The normal equations, their geometric meaning, and the first gradient method you will ever need.

blocks.text: The model, the loss, and the two ways in

With features $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ (a leading 1 absorbed for the intercept) and parameters $w \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the model is $\hat{y} = w^\top x$. Given $n$ examples in a design matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ and targets $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the squared-error objective is

payload.label: least squares
payload.note: The 1/2 is cosmetic: it cancels the exponent when differentiating.

payload.title: The normal equations

steps.text: Expand and differentiate using matrix calculus.
If $X^\top X$ is invertible, the unique stationary point is the global minimum, because $L$ is convex (its Hessian $\frac{1}{n}X^\top X$ is positive semidefinite).

payload.conclusion: Least squares has a closed form. It also has a geometry: $X w^\star$ is the orthogonal projection of $y$ onto the column space of $X$, so the residual $y - Xw^\star$ is orthogonal to every column — which is exactly $X^\top(Xw - y) = 0$.

blocks.text: When $d > n$ or columns are nearly collinear, $X^\top X$ is singular or ill-conditioned and the closed form is unstable. Ridge regression, $L(w) + \lambda \|w\|^2 / (2n)$, adds $\lambda I$ inside the inverse: a one-line fix with a bias–variance interpretation.

import numpy as np

X, y = load_design_matrix()          # X: (n, d), y: (n,)

# Closed form — fine for moderate d, and the reference answer to test against.
G = X.T @ X / len(y)
w_star = np.linalg.solve(G + 1e-8 * np.eye(G.shape[0]), X.T @ y / len(y))

# Gradient descent on the same objective.
w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
step = 1.0 / np.linalg.eigvalsh(G)[-1]   # 1 / largest eigenvalue of the Hessian
for _ in range(2000):
    grad = X.T @ (X @ w - y) / len(y)
    w = w - step * grad

print(np.allclose(w, w_star, atol=1e-6))

payload.caption: Both routes solve the same convex problem; the step size 1/L (L = top eigenvalue of the Hessian) is what makes the iterative route converge.

rows: Small d; exact answer; no tuning
Ill-conditioned X; numerically safer than forming XᵀX
Huge n or d; streaming data; the template for everything later
Large sparse problems with bad condition number κ
payload.caption: Same objective, different arithmetic. The course uses gradient descent because every later model is solved that way.

items: I can derive ∇L(w) = Xᵀ(Xw − y)/n without looking.
I can state the projection interpretation of the normal equations.
I can say why ridge stabilises an ill-conditioned design.

lessons.title: Gradient descent: why step size decides everything
lessons.summary: A quadratic model you can solve by hand, the exact divergence threshold, and an interactive you can break.

blocks.text: The update rule, and the only question that matters

Gradient descent is $w_{k+1} = w_k - \eta \nabla L(w_k)$. The gradient says *which way*; the step size $\eta$ says *how far*, and it is the parameter that decides between slow convergence, fast convergence, oscillation and divergence. To see this exactly, use the simplest non-trivial objective.

payload.note: A one-dimensional quadratic: convex, smooth, and solvable in closed form under iteration.

payload.title: Exact dynamics on a quadratic

steps.text: Write the error $e_k = w_k - w^\ast$ and substitute the update.
Convergence holds exactly when the multiplier has magnitude below 1.
The fastest choice kills the error in one step; beyond the threshold the error grows geometrically.
steps.note: For a quadratic with curvature c (L = (c/2)(w-w*)²) the thresholds rescale: 0 < η < 2/c, optimal η = 1/c.

payload.conclusion: On a smooth quadratic the whole story is one scalar multiplier. General smooth convex objectives behave the same way locally, with the curvature $c$ replaced by the Hessian's largest eigenvalue — which is why the code above used step = 1/L.

blocks.text: Push the learning-rate slider past $\eta = 1$ in the figure above: the iterates alternate sign and explode. That is not a bug in the simulation — it is the multiplier $(1-2\eta)$ exceeding 1 in magnitude. Real training runs show the same signature as a loss that suddenly becomes `nan`.

Two refinements you will meet everywhere. **Momentum** averages past gradients, which damps oscillation along high-curvature directions. **Adaptive methods** (AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam) scale each coordinate by its own gradient history, effectively choosing a per-coordinate step size — the practical default for deep networks, covered in `optimization-for-neural-networks`.

questions.prompt: On L(w) = (w − w*)², gradient descent with η = 1.2 produces…
questions.explain: The multiplier is 1 − 2η = −1.4, so |e_k| = 1.4^k |e_0| with alternating sign.

items: I can derive the exact convergence window 0 < η < 2/c for a quadratic of curvature c.
I can explain why 1/L (L = top Hessian eigenvalue) is a safe default step.
I can recognise divergence in a training log and name its cause.

modules.title: Choosing and checking models honestly
modules.summary: Model selection without self-deception: leakage, cross-validation schemes, and what to report.

lessons.title: Model selection and cross-validation without leakage
lessons.summary: Why the validation set must be untouched by every decision, and how to build one that is.

blocks.text: Three sets, three jobs

Fitting uses the **training** set. Choosing among models — hyperparameters, features, architecture — uses a **validation** set. Reporting a final number uses a **test** set that is opened exactly once. The moment a decision is made using test-set information, the test set has become a validation set and your reported number is optimistic.

**Leakage** is any path by which information from the evaluation data influences the fitted model: scaling features using whole-dataset statistics, imputing with global means, selecting features by full-data correlation, or tuning until the test score looks good. Each is invisible in the code and visible only in the protocol.

items: Split off the test set first and store it; do not look at it during development.
Inside the remaining data, run $K$-fold cross-validation: fit on $K-1$ folds, score on the held-out fold, average.
Put *every* data-dependent step — scaling, imputation, feature selection — inside the fold loop.
Pick the configuration by mean CV score; refit on all development data; evaluate once on the test set.

rows: Very large n; CV is unaffordable
The default; low-bias estimate of generalisation
Imbalanced classes; keeps class ratios per fold
Small n; averages over split noise
Duplicates or clusters (patients, users, time) must not straddle folds
Temporal data: train on the past, validate on the future
payload.caption: The scheme is part of the model. A random K-fold on clustered data estimates the wrong quantity.

blocks.text:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, cross_val_score
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

# Scaling lives INSIDE the pipeline, so each fold computes its own statistics.
pipe = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("ridge", Ridge())])
grid = GridSearchCV(pipe, {"ridge__alpha": [0.1, 1.0, 10.0]}, cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")
grid.fit(X_dev, y_dev)                    # development data only

print(grid.best_params_, -grid.best_score_)

model = grid.best_estimator_.fit(X_dev, y_dev)
print("test MSE (reported once):", ((model.predict(X_test) - y_test) ** 2).mean())

payload.caption: A pipeline keeps fold-local statistics local. Fitting the scaler on the full dataset before CV is the most common leakage bug in practice.

payload.problem: A team reports 0.94 AUC. Their script standardises features on the full dataset, then runs 5-fold CV, then tunes on the same CV, then reports the CV mean as the result. Name the two protocol errors and their direction.
steps: Full-data standardisation leaks fold-held-out information into training: optimistic bias, usually small but real.
Reporting the CV mean of the tuned configuration reuses the validation folds for selection: optimistic bias that grows with the number of configurations tried.
Neither error is visible in the final number; both are visible in the protocol.
payload.answer: Both errors inflate the reported score. Fix: pipeline-local preprocessing, and a nested CV or a held-out test set for the final figure.
payload.note: Nested CV: an outer loop estimates generalisation of the whole selection procedure, an inner loop does the selecting.

items: I can list three leakage paths and how to close each.
I can choose a CV scheme for clustered and for temporal data and justify it.
I can describe nested CV and say which quantity it estimates.
